product.title: Burmese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Burmese: the pronunciation is printed right above every word in Burmese script, with short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Burmese builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Also included: a table of the Burmese script and its vowel marks, a guide to the three tones and the breathy consonants, a list of Pali and English loanwords you already know, a table of classifiers, a summary of A1 sentence endings, and a glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up, from the word for "I" that changes with the speaker's gender to the ending တယ်, which is not a present-tense marker.

blocks.text: Burmese is almost always rejected before anyone tries it, and what puts people off isn't the grammar but **the shape of the letters**. People open the first page, see a row of circles like မြန်မာစကား, and close the book again, saying "no way". Yet the Burmese script is one of the **friendliest** parts of this whole journey. It's round because it used to be written on palm leaves — a straight line would split the leaf — so everything curves. There are thirty-three basic letters, and most of their sounds are easy for an English speaker. A determined learner can read it after a few sittings, not a few months.

The genuinely hard parts are elsewhere, and this book won't pretend otherwise. First, **Burmese has three tones**. ဆံ, ဆန်, and ဆမ်း aren't one word said three ways; they are three different words. Second, **the verb sits at the end of the sentence** and never stands alone: there's always a small ending after it — တယ်, မယ်, လား, ဘူး — and that ending is what tells you whether your sentence is a statement, a question, a negation, or a plan. Third, ⚠️ **the word for "I" depends on the speaker's gender**: men say ကျွန်တော်, women say ကျွန်မ. You'll use it in your very first sentence, so unit 1 covers it thoroughly.

The good news outweighs the bad by far. Burmese has **no articles**, **no grammatical gender**, and **verbs never change form** — မလာဘူး stays မလာဘူး whether it's I, you, or they who aren't coming. There isn't a single verb table to memorize. Plurals can even go unmarked. And counting has a pattern English speakers half know already: just as we say "two **loaves** of bread" or "three **head** of cattle", Burmese puts a counting word after every number — စာအုပ် သုံး အုပ်, "book three volume". The only difference is that Burmese does it for everything, and unit 6 shows you the handful you need.

There's one more gift that few Burmese textbooks mention: **you already know some Burmese words without ever having studied them**. ကံ is *karma*. ဓမ္မ is *dharma*. နိဗ္ဗာန် is *nirvana*. ဗုဒ္ဓ is *Buddha*. These came into Burmese from Pali, the language of the Buddhist scriptures, and into English through Buddhism and yoga. A second, newer layer came straight from English: ကား is *car*, ဖုန်း is *phone*, ကော်ဖီ is *coffee*. A special page in this book collects them, and the vocabulary lists flag them so you can stop for a moment and enjoy the recognition.

Three things are deliberately different from other Burmese books. First, **the pronunciation is printed directly above each Burmese word**, not on a separate line, so your eyes don't jump back and forth and lose their place mid-sentence. This isn't decoration: Burmese is written without spaces inside a phrase, and without the pronunciation above it a beginner will cut the words in the wrong places. Second, every line of dialogue has a **word-for-word translation** that shows the original order, even when it sounds strange — because that's exactly where the lesson is. Third, each unit targets **one classic trap for English speakers**, and names it openly instead of hiding it in a footnote.

One last thing. Fifty million people speak Burmese, and hardly any foreigners bother to learn it. So the reward comes very fast: say မင်္ဂလာပါ with the right tone to a stallholder at a Yangon market and watch what happens to their face. In a country rarely visited by people willing to make the effort, ten words are enough to get you treated as a guest, not a tourist.

This book is designed for self-study, without a teacher, in sessions of twenty to thirty minutes. One unit = one sitting. Don't do two units at once, even if it feels easy — Burmese builds up in layers, and a rushed unit will come back to haunt you in unit 12, where the sentence endings start stacking.
The recommended order within a unit

items: **Read the title and the list of goals.** Those five lines are the unit's promise. If by the end you can do all five without looking, the unit is done.

**Read the dialogue out loud, twice.** Once while looking at the pronunciation above the letters, and once more while covering the pronunciation with your finger and trying to read the Burmese script directly. It's the second round that teaches you the script — not the alphabet table.

**Read the tones, not just the letters.** A colon after a syllable means your voice starts high and falls, long; a period means it's cut short. If you ignore those marks, you're memorizing a different word from the one on the page.
**Only then read the translation.** Reversing this order is the most common mistake: if you read the meaning first, your eyes will never really look at the Burmese sentence.
**Pay attention to the literal line.** The small line under each sentence shows the original Burmese word order. That's where you learn to think in Burmese instead of translating from English.
**Do the exercises by hand, on paper.** Answering in your head feels faster and works far worse. The answer key is on the same page, so cover it with a sheet of paper first.

blocks.title: If you only have ten minutes today
items: Reread yesterday's dialogue out loud, then close the book. That's more useful than forcing yourself into a new unit when you're tired.
Once a week, redo the exercises of the last three units without looking at your notes. Whatever you've lost will show up immediately.
Practice the three tones with a single word: *sa.* — *sa* — *sa:* over and over while you're waiting for anything. Tones are only beaten by repetition; there's no shortcut.

blocks.text: The Burmese script is round not out of taste but because of the material. For centuries people in Myanmar wrote with a metal stylus on **palm leaves**, and a straight line drawn along the leaf's grain would tear it. So every shape was curved. Once you know that, the letters stop looking like a pile of bracelets and start looking like a family: ပ ဟ ဖ ဘ differ by a single stroke; so do င ဝ ဂ.

The second thing to know: **every consonant letter already carries the vowel *a***. က isn't "k" but "ka". မ isn't "m" but "ma". So မမ is read *ma.ma.*, and ကမ is read *ka.ma.*. You never write the *a* — it's been there from the start. Other vowels are attached as **small marks** to the right, left, top, or bottom of the letter, just like in Thai, Khmer, or the Devanagari script of Hindi. They are all relatives: descendants of the Brahmi script of ancient India.

The third thing, and the one that most often gets beginners lost: **Burmese puts no spaces between words**. Spaces separate parts of a sentence, roughly the way commas do in English. That's why the pronunciation in this book is printed right above the words, with hyphens between syllables — so you can see for yourself where one word stops and the next begins. The single vertical stroke ၊ is a comma, and the double stroke ။ is a period.
Watch how the letter က changes its sound just because of the small marks around it — and notice that the same mark also decides its **tone**:

blocks.title: ⚠️ Two letters that fool English speakers
items: **ရ is read *y*, not *r*.** Its shape does come from the old letter *ra*, but modern speakers pronounce it *y*: ရေ = *yay* (water), with no r at all. A trace of the *r* sound survives only in a few names and loanwords.

**သ is read *th* as in *think* — not *t*, and not *s*.** The tip of the tongue touches the back of the upper teeth and the air flows between them. သူ = *thoo* (he, she), not "too" and not "sue". Don't confuse it with *ht*, which is a breathy *t* (see the next page).

front.title: Three tones, breathy sounds, and the caught sound

blocks.text: This page is the key to the whole book. None of the three things on it work this way in English, and all three change meaning. Read it slowly and out loud, and come back here whenever a pronunciation confuses you.
1. Three tones

In English, pitch only carries feeling — surprise, doubt, boredom. In Burmese, pitch carries **meaning**. The same syllable can be three different words, and listeners won't guess from context — they genuinely hear a different word.

head: Tone
Marked
How it sounds
Example
rows: Short, cut off suddenly, as if the sound is caught in the throat. The shortest of the three.
Medium, level, neither rising nor falling. Normal length.
Starts high and falls, and is **longer** than the other two. It sounds slightly "pressed".

blocks.text: The classic practice set: **စ** *sa.* (begin) — **စာ** *sa* (writing) — **စား** *sa:* (eat). Say all three over and over until your hand starts moving along by itself. ⚠️ What English speakers miss most is the high tone, because the **း** mark is small and easy to overlook. Yet it's everywhere: ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ် alone has two.
2. Breathy sounds — h in front

Burmese distinguishes consonants that come out **plain** from consonants that come out **with a puff of air**. In this book the puff is marked with an **h in front** of the letter. English has both sounds but never contrasts them: the *p* in *pin* has a puff, the *p* in *spin* doesn't. The test: hold your palm in front of your mouth. If you feel air, it's the breathy sound. ⚠️ Plain *k, t, p, s* must have **no** puff at all — like the *p* in *spin*.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Don't read these as English letter pairs
items: *hp* isn't **f** but a **p** with a puff of air. ဖုန်း = *hpohⁿ:*, which sounds close to English "phone" — that's exactly where it comes from.
*ht* isn't English *th* but a **t** with a puff of air. The English *th* sound is used for the letter **သ**, and in this book it's written *th*, with no h in front.
*hs* isn't **sh** but an **s** with a puff of air. The Burmese *sh* sound is written ရှ.

blocks.text: 3. The caught sound — final k

Many Burmese syllables end with a sound that's **caught in the throat**: the breath stops suddenly and no consonant is actually released. English speakers already make this sound — it's the catch in the middle of **uh-oh**, or the *t* in a quickly said *button*. In this book it's always written **-k**, whatever silent letter the Burmese spelling uses (တ်, ပ်, က်, or စ်). ⚠️ Don't pop a real *k* at the end: stop the breath and let it go silent.
4. Nasal sounds — the small ⁿ

Syllables closed by န်, မ်, င်, or the mark ံ do **not** end with a clear n or m. Instead, the air goes out through the nose while the mouth stays open — like the vowel in French *bon*. This book marks it with a small **ⁿ**: မြန်မာ = *myaⁿ-ma*, ဖုန်း = *hpohⁿ:*, ကံ = *kaⁿ*. ⚠️ Don't close your lips at the end the way you do in "Sam" — keep the mouth open.

blocks.text: 5. Vowels at a glance

The spelling in this book is made for English readers: *a* as in *father*; *ee* as in *see*; *i* (only before -k or ⁿ) as in *sit*; *oo* as in *food*; *ay* as in *day*, but pure, without gliding into a y; *oh* as in *go*, pure, without a w at the end; *ow* as in *how*; *ai* as in *Thai*. Two vowels open the mouth **wider**: **è** as in *bed* and **ò** (also written *aw*) as in *law*. Both are very common: တယ် *dè* (the statement ending) and ကော်ဖီ *kò-hpee* (coffee) already contain one each. Consonants: *ch* as in *church*, *sh* as in *shoe*, *th* as in *think*, *dh* as in *this*, *j* as in *jam*, *g* always hard as in *go*, *ng* as in *singer* — even at the start of a word: ငါး *nga:*. *hm, hn, hny, hng, hl* are breathed: let a puff of air out before the m, n, ny, ng, or l.

A surprise is waiting for most beginners, and it's worth knowing from this page on so you can enjoy it from the first unit. **Burmese took hundreds of words from Pali, the language of the Buddhist scriptures** — a close sibling of Sanskrit. Many of those same words reached English through Buddhism, yoga, and Indian culture, so they arrive in Burmese in a form you can still recognize.
Here are the most common ones. Read them out loud and notice how many feel familiar:

blocks.text: The newer layer, straight from English
The second layer is much younger and even easier: words Burmese borrowed from English during the colonial era and after. You only need to adjust them to Burmese sounds.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Six words whose everyday meaning has shifted
items: **ဒေသ** *day-tha.* = **region, area** — not a village. ဒေသခံ = a local.
**ပညာ** *pyiⁿ-nya* = **knowledge or education**, a thing you get — not the mystical "wisdom" of yoga books. ပညာသင် = to go to school.
**ဂုဏ်** *gohⁿ* = **honor, dignity** — not the "qualities" (*guṇa*) of yoga philosophy.
**စိတ်** *sayk* = **mind and feelings** in general. စိတ်မကောင်းဘူး = sad.
**ကံ** *kaⁿ* = **luck** in everyday use, not a cosmic law of cause and effect. ကံကောင်းတယ် = lucky.
**ဒုက္ခ** *dohk-hka.* is used every day for **a hassle**, not deep suffering. ဒုက္ခပါပဲ ≈ "what a pain".

blocks.text: Whenever a word like this appears in a unit, the vocabulary list flags it. You don't need to memorize these — you only need to recognize them again, and that's far cheaper.

back.title: Classifiers: the list you'll actually use

blocks.text: Counting in Burmese follows one fixed order: **thing — number — classifier**. English does this only now and then ("bread, two loaves"); Burmese does it every time: စာအုပ် သုံး အုပ်, "book three volume". All you need to learn is the classifiers, and fewer than a dozen are really used at A1.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three things to remember when counting
items: **တစ် becomes တ- before a classifier.** တစ်ယောက် is read *ta.yowk*, not *tik-yowk*. The same happens to နှစ် → *hna.*, so နှစ်ခု is read *hna.hkoo.*
**The number 10 uses ဆယ် and sticks on too:** ဆယ်ယောက် *hsay-yowk* (ten people), နှစ်ဆယ့်ငါးယောက် *hna.hsay.nga:-yowk* (twenty-five people).
**To ask "how many", use ဘယ်နှစ် + classifier:** ဘယ်နှစ်ယောက်လဲ *bè-hna.yowk-lè:* (how many people?), ဘယ်နှစ်ခုလဲ (how many things?). For prices, use ဘယ်လောက်လဲ.

blocks.title: ⚠️ The three most common ending traps
items: **တယ် is not a "present tense" marker.** It marks something **real** — yesterday, this morning, or a habit. The time comes from time words in the sentence, not from the ending: မနေ့က စားတယ် = ate yesterday.
**Negation uses two parts at once:** မ before the verb **and** ဘူး after it. Forgetting one of them is the number-one beginner mistake.
**ပြီ and ပြီး are different.** ပြီ (*bee*) = "already, finally"; ပြီး (*pyee:*) = "finished, then". Tone and length tell them apart.

blocks.text: Burmese has **its own digits**, and they're still used every day — on license plates, market prices, bus numbers, and newspaper dates. They're easy to recognize because they're round like the letters.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Prices in Myanmar are almost always given in သောင်း and သိန်း
items: **၅ သောင်း** = 50,000 kyat — "five ten-thousands", not "fifty thousand" built the English way.
**၂ သိန်း** = 200,000 kyat. Tourists who count the zeros one by one always fall behind; learn to count in these units from the start.
The currency is the ကျပ် (*chak*), written Ks or K before the number.

blocks.text: Telling the time
Clock times use **number + နာရီ**, and the part of the day goes **in front**, not after the time as in "seven a.m.".

blocks.text: ⚠️ **ခွဲ means "and a half" — half past, never half to.** သုံးနာရီခွဲ is **3:30** — Burmese counts the hour that has **already passed**, just like English "half past three". British "half three" works the same way. Only learners who know German or Dutch, where "half four" means 3:30, need to watch out.

blocks.text: Like the English days (Sunday, Monday, Saturday), the Burmese days are named after the sun, the moon, and the planets — only here the names come from Sanskrit astrology, the same source as the day names in Thai, Khmer, and Javanese. The months follow the international calendar and are borrowed from English: ဇန်နဝါရီ, ဖေဖော်ဝါရီ, မတ်, ဧပြီ, မေ, ဇွန်, ဇူလိုင်, ဩဂုတ်, စက်တင်ဘာ, အောက်တိုဘာ, နိုဝင်ဘာ, ဒီဇင်ဘာ.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Questions with a question word end in လဲ, not လား
items: If the sentence contains a **question word** (ဘာ, ဘယ်သူ, ဘယ်မှာ…), the ending must be **လဲ**: ဘာစားလဲ — what are you eating?
If there's no question word and the answer is just "yes" or "no", the ending is **လား**: ထမင်းစားလား — are you eating rice?
Mixing the two up is the mistake a Burmese ear notices fastest — and the easiest one to fix.

blocks.text: If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, you hold something rare: the ability to read the Burmese script, about six hundred words, and the entire A1 sentence framework. That's enough to order food, bargain at the market, take a taxi to the right place, introduce yourself, and tell the story of a day that's gone by. What's missing isn't grammar — it's hours of practice.
The three things that raise your level most, in order

items: **Reread every dialogue in this book out loud, all twenty units, without looking at the pronunciation.** It sounds boring and pays off the most. The Burmese script only sticks through eyes that read it again and again, not through an alphabet table.

**Keep a three-sentence diary every day.** Where you went yesterday, what you ate, how it was. Three sentences, every day, in Burmese script. In a single month that's ninety sentences you built yourself.

**Find one person to talk to.** Burmese teachers are rare outside Myanmar, but there are large Burmese communities in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, the US, the UK, and Australia who are active online — and almost all of them are delighted to hear a foreigner try.

blocks.text: What awaits you at the next level

A2 in Burmese revolves around three things this book deliberately doesn't cover in full. First, **the written language, which differs from the spoken one** — newspapers, announcements, and books use their own set of words (သည်, ၏, များ, ခြင်း) that nobody says in the street. Second, **subordinate clauses**: linking two events with …တဲ့, …ရင်, …ပေမဲ့ until your sentences can run long without breaking. Third, **finer levels of politeness**, including how to speak to monks, which has its own vocabulary.

blocks.title: Before you leave for Myanmar
items: Take off your shoes **and socks** before entering a pagoda compound. The rule applies to the whole compound, not just the buildings.
Don't point at anything with your foot, and don't stretch your legs out toward a Buddha image or toward an older person.
The head is considered the most honored part of the body. Don't touch anyone's head, not even a small child's, however affectionate you mean to be.
Give and receive things with your right hand while your left hand touches your right elbow — a gesture of respect everyone recognizes.
**ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်** is said far less often than "thank you" in English, and precisely for that reason it sounds more meaningful. Use it, but not in every sentence.

blocks.text: ကံကောင်းပါစေ — *kaⁿ-kowⁿ:-ba-zay*, good luck. See you in the next book.
